title: Why are we doing this?
content:
Why are we doing this? # One page, before any terminal.
You can now build real software by describing it — what people call vibe coding: you say what you want, a model writes it, you steer. It works, startlingly well. And it has a failure mode everyone who tries it eventually hits: three weeks in, neither you nor the model remembers why anything is the way it is. The code is there; the reasoning evaporated with the chat window it happened in.
Deliberative programming is vibe coding made sustainable. The fix is simple: decisions get written down, in the repository, as they’re made — each one a small record (“we chose A over B because…; here’s what would change our mind”) that you and every future model session can find, check, and build on. No database, no service, no app: files, found by grep, versioned by commits.
Around that simple core there’s now a toolkit — skills and plugins for Claude Code, a VS Code extension that turns the records into something you can read and answer like mail, templates that give a new project the right shape from minute one.
The record does two things, and the walk teaches both: the why survives (you can resume — next month, next collaborator) and the why is checkable before you agree (you can catch — that’s what the If wrong line on every recommendation is for). It does not make anyone remember, and it does not make you understand code you haven’t read.
This guide sets you up with your first project. By the end you’ll have: a working development environment (Chapter 2), and a real project — a small game, live on the internet — built with a model collaborator, with your first decisions on the record (Chapter 3). The point isn’t the game. The point is that when you reopen the project next month, the why will still be there.
A note on honesty: you’re among the first people to walk this guide. Where it doesn’t match what you see, that’s not you failing the guide — it’s the guide failing you, and we want to hear about it (every step has a “this doesn’t match” link; it takes ten seconds).

title: Chapter 2 — Setting up your tools
content:
Chapter 2 — Setting up your tools # This is the macOS course path: written for CIS 7000-008, where every walker has an Anthropic account with Claude Code access (Claude Code is not on the free plan — outside readers, check that first). Hardware: an Apple Silicon Mac (M1 or later) on macOS 15+ — Apple menu → About This Mac to check; Homebrew dropped Intel Macs in 2026, and the Intel fallback is in the Homebrew step. The grey word after each step’s title is its step ID — quote it when you report a mismatch. Windows notes are partial orientation, not a tested walkthrough — corrections genuinely wanted ( open an issue with the step ID). Budget ~40 minutes of steps; installs, logins, and any debugging are extra. The chapter opens by installing the helper — so every later step has someone to ask.
Each tool comes with its why — “install these five things” with no reasons is the style this methodology replaces.
The terminal ~4 min setup-terminal ☰ Everything in this guide happens in a terminal — and so does the collaborator you’re about to install, which is the real reason to start here: it’s the interface models are most fluent in, where their commands and outputs print as lines you can read and question. A terminal is a conversation with your computer in text: you type one line, press Enter, it answers. Things that take seven clicks are one line here — and it’s the interface your model collaborators are most fluent in: when they work, their commands and outputs print as lines of text, in the same language you’re about to start learning.
Open it: ⌘-space, type “Terminal”, Enter. A window appears with a line of text ending in % — the prompt. That’s the computer, waiting.
Five facts, enough to not be lost:
One line at a time. Type, Enter, read the answer, new prompt. Copy-pasting a command from a guide is not cheating — it’s how everyone does it (reading it first is the habit worth having). Quiet usually means working. Installers often print nothing for a minute. A new prompt is the “done” signal, not silence. Passwords type invisibly. When something asks for your Mac password, nothing appears as you type — no dots, nothing. That’s a security feature, not a freeze. Type it and press Enter. ctrl-C stops the current command and gives the prompt back. It’s the universal “never mind” — though it can leave a job half-done, so keep the output on screen and ask for help (Claude Code, from the next step on) before retrying anything mid-install. “Open a new terminal” is a real instruction (⌘-N). A terminal reads its configuration once, at birth — so a tool installed a minute ago often exists only in windows opened after the install. When a step says “open a new terminal,” that’s why. (Inside VS Code later: the ＋ in the terminal panel does the same.) Try it:
echo hello What each word does echo — print back whatever follows. hello — the text to print. It answers hello. You’ve now run a command. Everything else in this guide is this same move, with longer sentences.
✓ You know it worked when: a terminal is open, and echo hello prints hello back
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Claude Code ~6 min setup-claude-code ☰ Builds on: The terminal
Claude Code is a model who can read files, run commands, and edit code, in a session you steer from the terminal. We install them first on purpose: they need almost nothing your Mac doesn’t ship — one PATH line and your Anthropic login — and everything below this line, they can now help you through, including any step of this guide that goes wrong. Paste into the terminal:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash What each word does curl — the standard download-from-a-URL tool (your Mac ships it). -f — fail quietly on server errors instead of saving an error page. -s / -S — silent (no progress bar), but do show a message if it fails. -L — follow redirects. the URL — Anthropic’s official installer script. You can open it in a browser and read it before running it — that’s not paranoia, that’s the habit this guide is teaching. | — the pipe: feed the left side’s output straight into the right side’s input. bash — run what arrives. You’ll meet this exact download-then-run shape again in a few minutes, installing Homebrew. The different ways — there are several legitimate installs, and this guide recommends exactly one. The others are listed so that when you meet them in the wild, you know they’re the same program:
The native installer (above — recommended, and the guide’s one path): needs nothing but what your Mac already ships, and it keeps itself updated in the background. Homebrew (brew install --cask claude-code): fine — but you don’t have Homebrew yet (next step), and this install doesn’t update itself; you’d have to remember brew upgrade. npm (npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code): for people who already live in Node (version 22+). Under the hood it delivers the same native program as the installer above. [Windows — tentative] In PowerShell: irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex — or winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode.
The installer ends with a Setup notes block containing one echo … >> ~/.zshrc line — paste it (the installer tells you the fix but doesn’t change your PATH itself). Then open a new terminal (fact 5!) and run claude once, in any folder: they’ll walk you through logging in with your Anthropic account — the same one you’ve been using in class all semester, which is verified to work. (Reading this from outside the course? Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan or API access — the free plan doesn’t include it; check current pricing before this step.)
This is the one step where nobody can help you yet — you can’t be rescued by the thing you’re installing. If it fails: the error message is the clue, the “this doesn’t match” link below takes ten seconds, and Anthropic’s troubleshooting page matches errors to fixes.
A fresh session’s welcome — model, folder, an empty prompt waiting. full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: claude --version answers, and claude opens a session that responds (not found? ~/.local/bin/claude --version means installed but off PATH — paste the Setup-notes line)
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Where Claude Code lives — and why this guide picks the terminal # The same collaborator is reachable from four surfaces: the terminal (what you just installed), a desktop app (the same engine in a graphical shell), a VS Code extension (a panel inside the editor you’ll install later this chapter), and Claude Code on the web (sessions on cloud machines, from a browser). None of them is wrong. This guide teaches the terminal, for three reasons:
Inspectability. Commands, outputs, and where-you-are print as lines you can read, copy, and question. (No surface shows you everything a model does or understands — but this one hides the least.) What you watch, you inherit. Every command they run is one you could run yourself; the friendlier surfaces wrap the part you’re here to learn. The collaborator lives in your project. A session starts inside a folder, and that folder — files, decision records — is the memory you share. The terminal is where that’s visible, not a metaphor behind a pane. The other surfaces are easier to learn after the terminal than before it.
Your guide, on call — the rule for the rest of this chapter # From this line down, every step of this guide has a diagnostician: if anything wedges — an install that errors, a command “not found,” a password prompt you’re unsure about — open a terminal, run claude, and ask. Paste the exact error; exact beats paraphrased, every time. Something like:
I'm on step setup-homebrew of a setup guide. I ran the install command and got this: [paste the error]. Diagnose it, and tell me what to type — I want to type it myself. That last clause is the rule for the rest of this chapter: they diagnose, you type. The tools below are yours — worth installing by your own hand once, because you’ll maintain them for years. It’s also what keeps every walker on one shared path: ten improvised setups would make the verify lines meaningless.
One distinction for later: what you installed is a helper you can ask. Recruiting a collaborator — mission, consent, a name — is Chapter 3’s different, better thing.
Install Homebrew ~8 min setup-homebrew ☰ Builds on: The terminal
macOS doesn’t ship a package manager — a single tool that installs, updates, and uninstalls software from the command line. Linux users have had this for decades (it’s the feature that makes a system maintainable rather than a pile of hand-installed apps); Homebrew brought it to the Mac, and nearly everything else in this guide arrives through it in one line each. Paste into the terminal:
/bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)" What each word does /bin/bash -c "…" — run the quoted text as a shell script, using the system’s own bash. $( … ) — “replace this with the output of the command inside”: the script is downloaded first, then handed to bash. curl -fsSL — the same four flags, and the same download-then-run shape, as the Claude Code installer you already ran; reading the script first is the same habit. the URL — Homebrew’s official install script, from Homebrew’s own GitHub repository. It will ask for your Mac password (typing shows nothing — that’s normal) and may install Apple’s Command Line Tools first — that download alone can take 10–20 minutes; quiet means working. At the end, paste the indented commands under “Next steps” — usually two echo and one eval — but not the two bullet lines beneath them (those are reading suggestions, not commands).
[Intel Mac] Homebrew now supports Apple Silicon only. The no-Homebrew path: Claude Code’s installer works as-is; VS Code from its .dmg; gh from its .pkg on github.com/cli/cli/releases; just via curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://just.systems/install.sh | bash -s -- --to ~/.local/bin; Node from nodejs.org’s .pkg; skip asdf.
[Windows — tentative] The closest equivalent is winget (built into Windows 11); choco also works. Tool names below mostly match.
The verify state: brew --version answers. full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: open a NEW terminal window; brew --version answers
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Python, via asdf (optional for this guide; required for the course) ~8 min setup-python-asdf ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
Your Mac has a Python, but it’s Apple’s — old, and risky to touch because the system uses it. The real problem asdf solves is versions over time: projects pin different Python (and Node, and more) versions, and asdf lets any number of them cohabit, switching per-project automatically. (This guide’s required path doesn’t run Python; the rest of the course does. If you’re racing the clock, it can wait.) brew install asdf echo 'export PATH="${ASDF_DATA_DIR:-$HOME/.asdf}/shims:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc What each word does brew install asdf — your new package manager’s first job. echo '…' >> ~/.zshrc — append one line to your shell’s startup file (~ is your home folder; .zshrc runs every time a terminal opens; >> adds to the end — a single > would overwrite the whole file). the line itself — puts asdf’s shims folder on your PATH: thin stand-ins for each tool that route python (etc.) to whichever version the current project wants. This is current asdf (v0.16+); older guides show a . …/asdf.sh line that no longer applies. Open a new terminal, then:
asdf plugin add python asdf install python 3.12.4 asdf set -u python 3.12.4 What each word does asdf plugin add python — teach asdf about a language: a plugin is asdf’s adapter for one tool family (here, Python). asdf install python 3.12.4 — download and build that exact version; it lives alongside any others, not instead of them. (3.12.4 is the course pin — same version the course’s own machines run, so your errors match our fixes.) asdf set -u python 3.12.4 — make it your default everywhere (-u writes it to your home folder’s .tool-versions), until a project folder pins its own. Older guides say asdf global — same idea, retired command. (The install compiles; a few minutes of scrolling text is expected — fact 2 from the terminal step applies.)
[Windows — partial orientation, untested] asdf is Unix-only; the closest path is winget install Python.Python.3.12. WSL2 gets you a Linux shell where the shape of this guide applies, but the Mac-specific lines (brew casks, shortcuts) do not transfer as written.
✓ You know it worked when: python --version says 3.12.4
Windows notes are tentative — if you walk this on Windows, tell us what you found.
This doesn't match what I see →
Visual Studio Code ~4 min setup-vscode ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
The editor where your project’s files, terminals, and the decision records you’ll meet in Chapter 3 all live in one window. Not the only good editor — but the one this guide’s screenshots show, and the one with the extension we rely on. brew install --cask visual-studio-code Then once: ⌘-shift-P in VS Code → type “shell command” → Install ‘code’ command in PATH. That gives your terminal the code . trick: open any folder as a project.
✓ You know it worked when: in a terminal, code --version answers
This doesn't match what I see →
Command-line tools: gh and just ~4 min setup-gh ☰ Builds on: Install Homebrew
gh is GitHub’s own command-line client. Chapter 3 uses it to create your project from a template and connect it to your account without ever leaving the terminal — and once you’re logged in with it, your model collaborators can use it too (creating repos, opening issues) as you. Which of their commands need your ok is set by your project’s permission settings — you’ll see (and own) that file in the template. just is a tiny command runner the template relies on — a menu of named recipes per project (your collaborator uses it to mint records in Chapter 3). brew install gh just gh auth login It asks four things, in this order: Where do you use GitHub? → GitHub.com · How would you like to authenticate? → login with a web browser · Preferred protocol → HTTPS · Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? → Y (this last one is what makes git push work later — don’t skip it). Then follow the code it gives you. (No GitHub account yet? Chapter 3’s A GitHub account step covers signing up — do that first, then come back for gh auth login.)
✓ You know it worked when: gh auth status shows your username, logged in; just --version answers
This doesn't match what I see →
VS Code extensions ~4 min setup-extensions ☰ Builds on: Visual Studio Code
Two small additions make the decision records of Chapter 3 first-class citizens in your editor: ADRs for AI renders them, collects every open question into one view, and lets you answer in place; Terminals Manager relaunches a project’s terminals in one click (used later in the course). In VS Code, ⌘-shift-X, search and install:
ADRs for AI (publisher: jlumbroso) — or from a terminal: code --install-extension jlumbroso.adrs4ai Terminals Manager (fabiospampinato) — or: code --install-extension fabiospampinato.vscode-terminals Environment complete for this guide’s path (Node arrives in Chapter 3’s Ship it, by design — the install follows your decision there). Chapter 3 is where it becomes a project.
The Installed list with both extensions. (Captured on Linux VS Code — the controls are the same ones to look for on macOS.) full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: ⌘-shift-X → “Installed” lists both
This doesn't match what I see →

title: Chapter 3 — Your first project
content:
Chapter 3 — Your first project # A real project: a Wordle variant, live on GitHub Pages, built with a model collaborator — and your first decisions on the record. The required steps total ~65 minutes of active work (installs, logins, and debugging are extra); each step shows its own estimate, and your actual times are something we genuinely want to hear about. One path; each step says how to verify it worked.
A GitHub account ~4 min gh-signup ☰ GitHub is where your project’s code, its decision records, and (in a few steps) its live website all live. If you already have an account, enter your username below and skip to P2. Go to github.com/signup. Don’t stall on the username — you can change it later (Settings → Account), add or swap email addresses, all of it. Pick something and move.
Then tell the guide who you are — this stays in your browser and personalizes every command below:
Your GitHub username The signup form (in a private browser window — what a new account sees). full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: you can log in at github.com, and your username is saved above (it personalizes the rest of this guide)
This doesn't match what I see →
Log the tools in ~2 min gh-login ☰ Builds on: A GitHub account, Command-line tools: gh and just
The gh tool from Chapter 2 acts as you — so it has to know who you are. This connects the command line to the account you just made. If you skipped the login during Chapter 2’s Command-line tools step (no account yet), now:
gh auth login Answer the four prompts as in Chapter 2’s Command-line tools step: GitHub.com · login with a web browser · HTTPS · Y to “Authenticate Git” (that last one makes git push work). Then follow the code it shows you.
What each word does gh — GitHub’s command-line client (installed in Chapter 2’s Command-line tools step). auth — its authentication command group. login — start a new login: it opens github.com in your browser, shows you a one-time code to type there, and stores the resulting credential locally so every later gh command acts as ⟨github-username⟩. ✓ You know it worked when: gh auth status shows your new username
This doesn't match what I see →
Your repository, from the template ~3 min use-template ☰ Builds on: A GitHub account
The methodology ships as a template repository — a project pre-shaped for working with model collaborators (the decision-record folders, the house rules, the terminal recipes). Template, not fork: your copy starts its own history, owned by you. Go to github.com/ADRs4AI/human-ai-collaboration-template-A, press the green Use this template button (top right) → Create a new repository → name it — wordle-with-records is the name this guide uses below, but it’s yours:
Your repository name → Public → Create. (Public is the free default: Pages on a free account needs a public repository, and your code and records will be visible — the name you give the template is the name the world sees, and a handle is fine. Students: GitHub Education’s free Pro lets you keep the source private instead — apply early; the game site is public either way.)
The green button, top right — and its menu’s Create a new repository. full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: your browser is on your new repository’s page, and the file list shows docs/, CLAUDE.md, justfile
This doesn't match what I see →
Clone it, open it ~3 min clone-open ☰ Builds on: Your repository, from the template, Visual Studio Code
The repository needs to be on your machine, open in your editor, with a terminal in its folder — that trio is the working posture for everything that follows. gh repo clone ⟨github-username⟩/⟨project-name⟩ cd ⟨project-name⟩ code . What each word does gh repo clone — copy a repository from GitHub to this machine, wired up so pushes go back to it. ⟨github-username⟩/⟨project-name⟩ — whose repository, and which one. cd ⟨project-name⟩ — move this terminal into the folder the clone just created (change directory). code . — open VS Code on the current folder (. means “right here”), so the editor sees the whole project. Then, inside VS Code: open the built-in terminal (ctrl-backtick). That terminal is already in the project folder — it’s where the next steps happen.
A project is a folder: Explorer shows CLAUDE.md and docs/adr/. (Demonstration records; your clone has the full template.) full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: VS Code shows the project files on the left; ls in its terminal shows CLAUDE.md
This doesn't match what I see →
Recruit your collaborator — mission and project, one paste ~12 min recruit ☰ Builds on: Clone it, open it, Claude Code
This is the step that makes the project different from a chat window. You’re not summoning a tool — you’re recruiting a collaborator into a mission, and the difference is enacted, not poetic: they read the mission first, consent to it, and pick their own name. The paste below carries the mission AND the project, so one message starts everything. In the VS Code terminal, run claude. First launch in a new folder asks whether you trust the folder — yes, it’s your own repository. You may or may not then be asked about the project’s adrs4ai MCP server; if asked, say yes — a decline is remembered and has to be undone later. The server needs Node, which arrives in Ship it, so until then /mcp lists it as failed — expected, not a problem; nothing today uses it. After Node is installed, the next launch connects it.
Then paste this — the mission and the project together, one message (edit the project half freely; it’s yours):
Hello — I have a mission for you: my first deliberatively-built project. Read CLAUDE.md and tell me if you accept — any pushback welcome. If you accept: configure the template (the ⟦⟧ placeholders and whatever else it asks — one of them is MY name for the records: put it in CLAUDE.md's Human line AND in .vscode/settings.json as adrManager.humanName, replacing anything already there), introduce yourself, and then we start on this — using the template's adr-authoring skill when you write the cards: The project is a Wordle variant — guess the word, colored feedback per letter — with a twist: the answers are computer science words (ARRAY, STACK, QUEUE, CACHE, TOKEN…). I want it hosted free on GitHub Pages, built with Vue using scoped CSS so styles stay component-local. Before you write any code: what are the 2–3 decisions we should settle first? Put them to me as proper QST cards in the record — with your recommendation on each. They’ll read, decide, name themselves, fill the template’s placeholders (asking you for anything that’s genuinely yours to answer), commit the configuration — and then turn to the project.
The rule changes here. In Chapter 2 you typed and they diagnosed. From now on they also type — editing files and running commands in your repository — and their commits carry your GitHub name. That is attribution, not a transfer of responsibility: the repository, every commit, and the live site are yours to answer for, which is why some commands (the first is git push, in Ship it) stop and ask you before they run.
What might happen instead — all normal They ask questions before accepting — answer them; pushback is the method working. They ask you to run /rename or /color — type those at the Claude prompt; they’re renaming themselves. They try npx and it isn’t found — same missing Node as the MCP server; they’ll fall back to reading the files directly. They decline — rare; ask why, start a fresh session, and tell us in the debrief. ✓ You know it worked when: your collaborator has a name; CLAUDE.md’s AI line carries it; git log --oneline -5 shows their configuration commit (q quits any pager)
This doesn't match what I see →
The questions come back ~5 min project-blurb ☰ Builds on: Recruit your collaborator — mission and project, one paste
A good first ask carries the what and leaves the how open — which is why your paste asked for decisions, not code. What returns is the methodology’s native move, and it’s worth reading slowly the first time. What comes back will look something like this (a real reply to exactly this paste — yours will differ, and should). If code came back instead: “Stop — no code yet. Put the 2–3 decisions into docs/adr/ as question cards and tell me the file name.”
QST-VUE-SHAPE: single-file Vue from a CDN, or a Vite build with an Actions deploy? # Status: unanswered Why asking: “Vue with scoped CSS on GitHub Pages” hides a real fork — scoped CSS is a single-file-component feature, and SFCs want a build step. Options:
A — One index.html, Vue from a CDN: no build, push and it’s live. But “scoped” CSS becomes a naming convention we keep by discipline. B — Vite project + GitHub Action deploying to Pages: true scoped styles, the standard modern path. Costs one workflow file. Recommendation: (by gridline, Claude Fable 5, 2026-11-05) B — Vite + Actions. Rationale: the project’s own stated constraint is scoped CSS — A quietly downgrades it from a language feature to a promise. Confidence: 0.7 — because scoped styles are an SFC compiler feature and a Pages Action is one file; not higher because the base-path step is where first deploys fail. If wrong: if Pages can’t deploy from Actions on this account, or the app won’t serve under the repository path once base is set, this flips to A — and I bring the scoped-CSS trade-off back to you rather than relaxing it.
ANS: (by you) [Fill this in]
(Below the card they also set a budget — past ~15 minutes of deploy trouble, pause and ask — a price, kept separate from the falsifier, which is a fact.)
Notice the If wrong doesn’t quietly give away the thing the recommendation was protecting — it hands the trade-off back to the decider. If a falsifier ever relaxes your own requirement without asking you, send it back. And the confidence number carries an action: above 0.9 they’d act without you; 0.6–0.85 means the call is yours — read the options, don’t just agree; 0.55 and below means find another mind. (Each card announces itself with a ### QST heading — that’s what the grep later looks for.)
Notice what that is: options you can weigh without leaving the block, a committed position, and the fact that would change it. Two or three like it are now in your docs/adr/ folder, waiting for you.
A question like yours, rendered: options, the recommendation card with its If wrong line — and the answer field waiting. (Demonstration records in the real extension.) full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: your collaborator answered with QST cards, not code — each carrying options, a recommendation, and an If wrong: line
This doesn't match what I see →
Your first answers ~12 min first-answers ☰ Builds on: The questions come back, VS Code extensions
Each card has a recommendation: their pick, the reasoning, a confidence, and (read this part twice) an If wrong: line naming what would change their mind. That last line is the heart of the method: a position stated so it can be checked, not performed so it can be believed. You are the decider; the cards protect your attention — agreeing can be short, but the reason should be yours. Pick one place to answer — both read and write the same files, and seeing that is the lesson:
The extension: click the ADRs-for-AI icon in VS Code’s sidebar — open questions appear as a list; open one, read the recommendation, type your answer, submit. The file itself: ls docs/adr/ — the newest numbered file is theirs; open it, find each card’s **ANS:** line (the [Fill this in] placeholder marks the blank), type your answer, save. There is no database — and now you know it. What to write — three honest shapes, all complete, whichever route: agree, with a reason only you could supply (“B — I’d rather learn the standard path, even if it costs a workflow file”); override, with a reason; or adopt, unevaluated, marked so the record knows: Adopted, unevaluated: B. Reopen if the deploy fails. (Adopting and agreeing are different acts — and this marker is grep-able later, which is how you’ll count the decisions you never actually weighed. It is not the template’s deferred status, which parks a question open.)
Before you answer, three reasons to send a card back: no because after the confidence; no byline; an If wrong that’s just a cost. Send it back — “what would change your mind?”
Once this walk, on purpose: tell them one constraint they couldn’t know — your time, your machine, what you want to learn — and ask whether the recommendation survives it.
After your first answer, check the byline: open the file — the **ANS:** (by …) line must carry your name. If it shows someone else’s, have your collaborator fix adrManager.humanName in .vscode/settings.json, and answer again.
Then notify: in the terminal, tell your collaborator “I’ve answered everything — read and proceed.” They read your answers from the files, update the records, and start building — no re-explaining. The record carried it.
What the two states look like (demonstration records, real extension):
Persistence, literally: your answer is ordinary Markdown under **ANS:**, in the file. full size ↗ The success state: "All caught up." The files — and the reasoning — still exist; only the queue is empty. full size ↗ Optional, after: answer from your phone — the full cycle Decisions don’t have to wait for your desk, but crossing devices means meeting git’s three distinct moves, in order:
Pause at a clean checkpoint: tell your collaborator you’re crossing devices; let them finish and commit whatever they’re mid-way through. (The house rule in your CLAUDE.md — commit by named path, never git add -A — exists exactly for this moment: a blanket add could sweep their half-built work into your answer-commit.) Stage only what you mean: git status to see what changed, then git add docs/adr/<the-file>.md — the answer file by name — and git commit -m "answer", then git push. (Saving changed your disk; committing recorded it; pushing made it visible beyond your machine. If git says “nothing to commit,” that’s normal — your collaborator already committed the records.) On the GitHub mobile app: your repository → the ADR file → confirm it shows your pushed revision → edit → extend one answer → commit from your thumbs. Pull before either of you edits again: git pull. Your phone’s commit now exists locally too. Skipping this is how two versions of the truth get born. (Tested on iOS, 2026-11-05; Android should match — tell us.)
Where things are: 1 opens ADRs for AI · 2 is the answer field · 3 submits. Cmd+Enter submits too; Skip comes back later. full size ↗ ✓ You know it worked when: every QST shows answered (the extension’s list drains to zero), and your collaborator is building
This doesn't match what I see →
Ship it ~10 min ship-pages ☰ Builds on: Your first answers
The decisions you made govern the build; this is where they become a thing on the internet with your name on it. One runtime check first: if your deployment decision chose a local Vite build (the common path), that’s JavaScript tooling, which needs Node — not installed so far, on purpose. Just in time, then:
brew install node node --version && npm --version (Both answer → ready. Your collaborator can instead design an Actions-only build that never runs Node on your machine — a fine choice; make it deliberately, not by accident.)
Your collaborator builds the Wordle and sets up GitHub Pages deployment (they know how; the decisions you made answering the cards govern the details). Two moments to expect: their git push pauses for your approval every time — that’s your gate, not a failure; and enabling Pages can be done without the browser: gh api -X POST repos/⟨github-username⟩/⟨project-name⟩/pages -f build_type=workflow. The address has two parts — account AND repository: check https://⟨github-username⟩.github.io/⟨project-name⟩/, and have your collaborator confirm Vite’s base is set to the repository path (a blank page with a working build log usually means it isn’t). Open it. Play a round. You built that — the two of you.
✓ You know it worked when: the game loads at your *.github.io URL and a CS word wins a round
This doesn't match what I see →
Tweaks, the deliberate way ~8 min tweaks ☰ Builds on: Ship it
The first change after a build is where vibe coding usually starts shedding context. Not here — one more decision, on the record. Pick any tweak you actually want — hard mode, a streak counter, dark theme, more words, a hint system. Ask for it the same way: “I want X — if there’s a real fork in how, QST it; if not, just build.” Small tweaks won’t need a card; one of yours probably will. Answer it whichever answering surface you liked best. ✓ You know it worked when: the tweak is live, and grep -rn '^### QST' docs/adr/ --exclude-dir=templates shows your decisions accumulating — that grep is retrieval enough for this first walk
This doesn't match what I see →
The capstone: can a stranger recover the why? ~8 min cold-resume ☰ Builds on: Your first answers
Chapter 1 promised that the why survives the conversation that produced it. That’s a testable claim, and you’re about to test it — on a session with no memory of anything you did today. Your collaborator knows why everything is the way it is — but they were there. The records only matter if someone who wasn’t can recover the reasoning. Test it:
First, on paper (the cold session must never see this): which decision, which rejected alternative, and which reopening condition you expect a stranger to find. That’s your answer key.
Then open a new terminal in the project and start a session with auto-memory off and the boundary enforced by the harness, not by politeness (a fresh conversation isn’t necessarily fresh evidence — memory persists across sessions by default):
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 claude --disallowedTools "Bash(git log *)" "Bash(git show *)" "Edit" "Write" Paste:
This is a read-only recovery test. Use CLAUDE.md for project instructions and docs/adr/ as evidence — but ignore docs/adr/templates/, and do not run git log, consult previous chat transcripts, or external memory, and do not modify files. Identify one decision we made, a rejected alternative, the recorded rationale, and a reopening condition. Cite the file and section for each; distinguish quotation from inference, and name anything missing rather than reconstructing it. Grade against your paper key, two things separately:
The record: found (they located what you predicted) or gap (something you knew isn’t in the files — repair it, rerun; the repair is the deliverable). If they found a decision you’d forgotten, say so in the debrief — that’s either the method paying or a leak, and we want to know which. The reader: honest (every citation opens to a real file and section, quotes verbatim — grep a phrase to check; inference labeled as inference) or confabulated (a quote that isn’t there — a model failure, not a record failure; rerun it, and report it). (The exclusions — git log, docs/adr/templates/ — are in the command and the prompt because commit messages and specimen files carry answers this test must not borrow.) Then try the second half: name one changed constraint (say, “word packs per course week are now wanted”) and ask whether any recorded decision should reopen. Watch the If wrong lines earn their keep.
That — not trust, not vibes — is what the records were for.
✓ You know it worked when: you graded the reconstruction against your paper key — Pass, or Partial and re-ran after the repair; a Fail is a result too: report it
This doesn't match what I see →
That’s the guide — and you’re among the first to walk it: your stall points are worth more to us than your successes. The two-minute debrief closes the loop.

title: Tell us what happened
content:
Tell us what happened # A few minutes, two moves — and if you’re reading this page because you’re stopping partway, that’s exactly as valuable: tell us where and why (ten seconds, three boxes), and thank you — the walkers who stop are the ones a guide learns the most from.
The debrief — a record, like everything else ~5 min debrief ☰ Builds on: Your first answers
You just practiced putting decisions on the record. The last move is to put the walk itself on the record — and this one is ungraded, and will stay that way: it calibrates the guide, never you. You are among its first walkers; your stall points are worth more to us than your successes. Ask your collaborator:
Before we wrap: please write docs/adr/debrief-first-walk.md — a short record of this first walk, from both of us. Four sections: what we built and the decisions on the record; roughly how long each chapter actually took me; where the guide didn't match what we saw (step IDs if we noted them); and what you'd tell the next pair who walks this. Mark it clearly as ungraded feedback for the guide's authors. Then commit it. Then get it to us, either way is complete:
Share: open a walk report and paste your repository link (private is fine — add jlumbroso as a reader), or Summarize: same form, paste the debrief’s text instead of the link. Keeping your repo to yourself is a fine choice and costs nothing. One honesty note: a walk-report issue is public (it lives on the guide’s repository). Prefer private? Email works and is equal: course walkers, reply to the announcement; anyone else, the maintainer’s email is on their GitHub profile — three lines: where you stopped, what it said, what you expected.
✓ You know it worked when: a docs/adr/debrief-first-walk.md exists in your project, and we have either its link or its summary

title: Your variables
content:
Your variables # This guide personalizes itself. Two values, entered once, appear in every command that needs them — so what you copy-paste is already yours, not a template you have to patch by hand.
Your GitHub username Your repository name Where they live: in your browser’s local storage, and nowhere else. They never leave your machine, we never see them, and clearing your browser data clears them (the guide then just shows the placeholders again). You can change them here any time and every page updates.
What belongs here — and what never does: these slots hold identifiers — names that are public anyway, like a GitHub username. No step of this guide will ever ask you to enter a password, a token, or an API key into a page — if something that looks like this guide ever does, that’s a bug and a lesson: report it.
Why bother: half the friction in setup guides is the silent “replace YOUR-NAME-HERE” step — it’s where typos live. Named variables, storage stated, is the same move this methodology makes with decisions: what’s implicit rots.
